name: Confessor Ivo Marrant
appearance: A Confessor in his forties in the grey cloak of his order, who puts his hood back in the cold so that his bald head is bare to the snow: a pleasant, well-fed face and a smile he gives to a whole court at once. He carries the iron censer on its chain in his own hand, so that he stands in his own grey weather, and the smell of hot iron reaches a gate ahead of his voice. At the bars he held nothing but the censer and the writ.
last_seen_doing: Going down the first flight of the Steps into the dusk with the censer and four grey cloaks, to make his fire on the lower terrace, having called up for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel and said he would wait.
now: Camped on the lower terrace below the gate of Saint Ysolde's, the law's ground and nobody's, with four grey cloaks; a fifth keeps the winch-house at the foot of the Steps. He has read his list at the bars under the Knight-Confessor's seal, Darrow first and Hollis second, been answered by Old Mercy and the law of names, and has said he will wait.
story_so_far: He led the grey cloaks up the Holloway and the Thousand Steps and came to the gate of Saint Ysolde's in the hour before dusk, with the censer in his hand. He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless had gone down the far side a week since, and read his list to the House anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand. When the Prior had the wicket opened a hand's width for his paper, two of his men came through it and were put back out by the House's shoulders as Old Mercy rang, and Mother Ione gave him the law's other half: no name under the bell is taken down against its will. He thanked her for her candour, said bells grow tired, and made his camp on the lower terrace, calling up for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel.

known_facts.fact: He came to the bars with four grey cloaks in the hour before dusk; the fifth had stayed at the winch-house with his boots on a cart.
He named himself to the Prior as Ivo Marrant, Confessor, under the Knight-Confessor's seal, as if they had corresponded.

He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless of Harrow Ford went down the far side a week since, and read anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand.
known_facts.evidence: I find it steadies the hand.

known_facts.fact: He unrolled the writ against the bars so the court could see its seal, blue wax the size of a child's palm, and read Darrow's name first and Hollis's second, then the Ninth's names and the Sixth's, slow, so the court could count.
known_facts.evidence: slow, so the court could count

known_facts.fact: He did not read the far cots, and said so himself: the Crown has no quarrel with men who can't answer.
known_facts.evidence: The Crown has no quarrel with men who can't answer.

known_facts.fact: He asked for the writ to be taken at the wicket under the law of guests, as a courier's paper; when the leaf opened a hand's width, two of his men put their shoulders into it and came through.
known_facts.evidence: two grey cloaks put their shoulders into it

known_facts.fact: What Darrow read in him at the bars: a fire, all of it poured, and under the pouring nothing of his own; no lie in him, and the wicket already open in his mind.
known_facts.evidence: nothing of his own at all

known_facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang and the Prior spoke the law of names, his eyes went past her shoulder to Maelis and stayed there a beat longer than courtesy, and his smile changed its weight.

He thanked the Prior for her candour, called his two men back through the wicket, and said the grey below the gate where the springs steam is the law's ground and nobody's: they would make their fire on the lower terrace, and bells grow tired.

He called up for Ser Darrow by name to the whole court, as a man says a name he is sure of: come down and kneel, and the rest of the paper goes back into his cloak and never comes out; he would wait, it is the thing he is best at.
known_facts.evidence: It's the thing I'm best at.

relationships.label: the Prior who answered his writ with the bell
relationships.note: She let him read, had the wicket opened for his paper under the law of guests, and when his men came through it Old Mercy rang and she gave him the law of names; he thanked her for her candour.

relationships.label: the first name on his paper
relationships.note: He read Darrow's name first at the bars without knowing his face among the wounded, and called up for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel, saying he would wait.

relationships.label: the Mender at the Prior's shoulder
relationships.note: When the bell was rung his eyes went to her and stayed a beat longer than courtesy, and she gave him nothing back.
